What it covers

The commercial one. Mason opens on the SEC disclosure rule that took effect the previous month, four business days to disclose a breach, and argues the follow-on pressure lands on SMB suppliers rather than only on public companies. From there it is the MSP business case: tool sprawl is the cost centre, proving compliance is the hard part, and CIS Level 1 and 2 remediations are a prepackaged service that can be sold the next day. Graham's demo shows a multi-tenant console, a SOC 2 audit at 93.4% patch efficacy, and remediation content deployed at scale. Notes

A session for service providers, with Mason Johnson, on turning regulatory pressure into billable work rather than overhead.

Mason opens on the SEC disclosure rule and the pressure it puts on suppliers. The interesting part of that argument is that it does not stop at public companies. A public company has to disclose within four business days, which means everyone it depends on now gets asked to demonstrate their own controls, whether or not they are regulated themselves.

What it covers

The economics for a managed service provider. Tool sprawl is the cost centre: separate products for patching, scanning and configuration, each with its own agent, its own training, and its own reports that someone has to reconcile by hand. Consolidating those is a margin story before it is a security story.

Then the commercial argument. Proving compliance is the hard part, and prepackaged remediations for CIS benchmarks and Microsoft STIGs turn that difficulty into a service that can be sold and delivered immediately rather than a project that takes a quarter to scope.

Worth watching

My demo section, which runs against a multi-tenant console rather than a single environment, because that is the shape of the problem for this audience. A SOC 2 audit lands at 93.4% patch efficacy, and the honest framing of a number like that matters more than the number.

The Q&A is worth keeping. Handling customers across twenty-three time zones with one maintenance window instead of twenty-three schedules, and the answer on how long the workflow builder takes to learn, which is two to three hours. That is a real adoption number and it is more useful than a feature list.

Sep 2023 · Solo presenter, live product demo

Spotlight Webinar: Autonomous Defense

Runtime
20:32
Series
Spotlight Webinar

What it covers

Builds a full defense-in-depth stack as a single Cortex workflow, layer by layer: firewall enabled, then the agent itself, then antivirus, then VPN, then a SIEM agent, then patch scan and deploy, then a vulnerability scan filtered to CVSS 8 and above. The argument underneath it is that attackers triage, and an organisation that is expensive to enter gets skipped rather than defeated. The second half is the operational discipline the workflow needs to survive contact with reality: publish as a policy rather than a one-shot task, pick an interval that does not melt endpoints, scope by location, and benchmark non-compliance month over month so improvement is measurable.

Notes

Building a full defense-in-depth stack as a single workflow, layer by layer, and then the operational discipline it needs to survive production.

The opening argument is about attacker economics. Most threat actors are not targeting anyone in particular. They scan, find nothing they can reach easily, and move on to the next organisation. Being expensive to enter is a real defensive strategy, and it is measurable in a way that "we have not been breached" is not.

What it covers

The stack assembled in one workflow: firewall enforced, then the agent itself, then antivirus, then VPN, then log collection, then patch scan and deploy, then a vulnerability scan filtered to the critical end of the CVSS range. Each layer is one node on the canvas, and the workflow is the whole posture in one readable object rather than seven consoles.

The second half is the part most automation conversations skip. A policy is only useful if it runs on a cadence the endpoints can tolerate, is scoped to the right assets, and produces a number someone can watch move month over month.

Worth watching

The exchange about intervals. Running a thousand compliance checks every thirty minutes is a good way to make an endpoint slow enough that users notice, and the honest answer to "how often" turns out to be a tradeoff rather than a best practice. Choosing twelve hours and saying why is a better answer than choosing the most aggressive option available.

Then the reporting section, which makes the argument that a compliance programme without a baseline is not a programme. Pick a metric, take a monthly snapshot, and hold yourself to a target. Twenty-five percent fewer non-compliant items each month is the example, and the point is that it is falsifiable.

Aug 2023 · Solo presenter, live product demo

Spotlight Webinar: Harnessing Automation

Runtime
20:48
Series
Spotlight Webinar

What it covers

Explicitly scoped away from patching and vulnerability remediation, which the series had already covered, to the rest of the automation surface: service control, access control, and software provisioning. Graham builds a drag-and-drop workflow live, starting with a Chrome-then-Teams install chain, then packaging CrowdStrike Falcon, then BitLocker enforcement with a branching path and a firewall check. The demo turns on a Print Spooler scenario where a stopped service triggers a firewall rule that blocks a DNS server, then flips back when the service returns. The closing move is the one that matters: adding a step that starts the service again so the policy heals the environment instead of just gating it. Ends on a 20-step Log4j server remediation that touches AWS elastic load balancer queues and EC2 snapshots.

Notes

Deliberately scoped away from patching, which the series had already covered, to the rest of the automation surface: service control, access control, and software provisioning.

The whole session is one live build, which is the right format for this argument. Talking about drag-and-drop automation is unconvincing. Watching a workflow go from an empty canvas to enforcing a policy in about six minutes is the actual claim.

What it covers

A provisioning chain first, installing one package and then another on the condition that the first succeeded, then packaging something bespoke that needs its own installer flags. From there, BitLocker enforcement with a branching path, and a firewall check with its own branch. The canvas handles the decision tree, which is the part that normally means opening an editor and debugging a script.

The interesting turn is the enforcement demo. A stopped service triggers a firewall rule that blocks access to a DNS server, and restoring the service releases it. That is gating, and gating alone is only half a policy.

Worth watching

The last few minutes, where the workflow gains a step that starts the stopped service back up. Once that is in place the policy heals the environment instead of locking people out of it, which is the difference between an enforcement tool and something a service desk can live with.

The closing example is a Log4j remediation on a server that runs to roughly twenty steps: opening a ticket, snapshotting a VM, draining it from an AWS elastic load balancer, patching Apache, revalidating, and putting it back. It is the answer to anyone who thinks no-code means shallow.

Mar 2023 · Solo presenter, live product demo

Spotlight Webinar: Vulnerability Remediation

Runtime
26:25
Series
Spotlight Webinar

What it covers

The most teaching-heavy of the Spotlight series. Graham spends the first ten minutes on vocabulary before touching the console: what a vulnerability actually is, how CVE assigns identity, how CVSS scores impact, and why the industry splits findings into patch vulnerabilities and configuration vulnerabilities. He uses Follina as the case that breaks the distinction, since Microsoft 365 support diagnostics was a configuration mitigation until a patch arrived to fix the configuration. The demo then follows a real remediation loop on three live findings, and closes on the argument that remediation should be policy-driven rather than pushed ad hoc, with the GPO comparison as the contrast.

Notes

A working session on the vocabulary first and then the mechanics: what a vulnerability is, how CVE and CVSS organise the problem, and why remediation has to be policy-driven rather than pushed by hand.

The first ten minutes are deliberately slow. Most remediation conversations go wrong because the participants are using the same words for different things, so this one starts with definitions: a vulnerability as a weakness that compromises integrity, availability or confidentiality, CVE as the identity framework, and CVSS as the thing that ranks severity.

What it covers

The split between patch vulnerabilities and configuration vulnerabilities, which is the distinction that decides how a remediation programme gets resourced. A patch is a package you deploy. A configuration finding is a change to how something already works, and it usually needs a different team and a different change process.

Follina is the case that breaks the neat division. Microsoft 365 support diagnostics was a configuration mitigation until Microsoft shipped a patch that fixed the configuration itself, which is a good illustration of why a findings list is a moving target rather than a fixed work queue.

Worth watching

The live remediation on three real findings: a disabled password complexity requirement, DNS resolver spoofing, and automatic sign-in after a system-initiated restart. Each gets the same treatment, which is the point. Scan, confirm, remediate, revalidate, and only then report it closed.

The closing argument is about delivery method. Pushing remediation as an ad hoc task is not repeatable and degrades over time. Running it as a policy means the environment holds its shape without anyone remembering to check. That is also where the comparison to group policy comes in, and why an agent that works regardless of network position changes what is possible.

Jan 2023 · Two-person interview, no demo

Analyst Insights: Advancing Zero Trust Priorities

Runtime
50:05
Series
Analyst Insights

What it covers

The outlier of the set and the strongest piece in it. No demo, no console, no product. Graham interviews Chris Steffen of EMA, who co-chairs the Cloud Security Alliance's zero trust working group, and the conversation is about the discipline rather than the tooling. Chris's central claim is that zero trust is a philosophy and not a product, that nobody sells an out-of-the-box zero trust solution, and that most organisations are already further along than they think because the compliance projects on their plate already contain the components. The recurring fictional example, Henry's House of Paper Clips, carries the argument about passed-down compliance and vendor due diligence. The closing third is the part worth quoting: the difference between checkbox compliance and audit-ready, why showing 100% compliance invites a deeper audit, and what a security leader can actually put in front of a C-suite that is looking for a finished project in a discipline with no finished state.

Notes

A conversation rather than a demo, recorded with Chris Steffen of Enterprise Management Associates, who co-chairs the Cloud Security Alliance zero trust working group.

This one is deliberately not a product session. There is no console and no walkthrough, because the honest version of the argument is that zero trust is a philosophy and not something you buy. Chris opens by saying he has never encountered an all-in-one zero trust solution, and that once you dig into what the term actually means, you can see why one cannot exist.

What it covers

Where organisations actually are, which is further along than most think. The compliance projects already on the calendar contain most of the components: identity, device management, data security, logging. The work is joining them up rather than starting over.

Then the distinction that carries the second half, between checkbox compliance and being genuinely audit ready. Those are different standards, and the audit-ready posture is the one that stops every audit being an emergency.

Worth watching

The passage on passed-down compliance, which explains why a twelve-person company now gets asked for a security plan by a customer that has never asked before. Chris walks through it with a paper clip manufacturer as the example, and the logic lands because it is not about the paper clips. It is about the connection into someone else's network.

Also the exchange on measurement. A dashboard that reports critical findings going up and down during the day is not evidence that the security team is failing. It is evidence that the environment changed. Knowing which of those two you are looking at is most of the job of presenting security to a leadership team.

Jul 2022 · Two presenters, one deck, long Q&A

The Cyber Kill Chain Masterclass

Runtime
54:39
Series
Syxsense Master Class

What it covers

A structured walk through the Lockheed Martin Cyber Kill Chain as a defensive planning tool rather than an attacker's checklist. Graham takes the eight phases one at a time and pairs each with the control that buys back time, from NIDS and NIPS at reconnaissance through HIDS at delivery, vulnerability management at exploitation, SIEM and the SOC at installation, segmentation and DNS sinkholes at command and control, and tested offline backups plus cyber insurance at actions on intent. The through-line is that the kill chain is not a sequence you either stop or fail, it is a clock, and every control that adds a phase transition is time your team gets back.

Notes

The monthly Syxsense Master Class, presented with Rob Brown, working through the Lockheed Martin kill chain phase by phase.

The framing I kept coming back to is that the kill chain is not a sequence you either stop or fail. It is a clock. Every control that adds a phase transition is time the response team gets back, and time is the only thing that reliably helps. That reframes the whole exercise from buying products to buying minutes.

What it covers

The eight phases, from reconnaissance through to actions on intent, and the control that buys back time at each one. Network intrusion detection and prevention on the perimeter, host intrusion detection at delivery, vulnerability management at exploitation, log aggregation and a SOC at installation, segmentation and DNS sinkholes at command and control, and tested offline backups plus cyber insurance at the end.

Worth watching

The section on counterfeit authentication, which is the difference between a user approving an install they asked for and a user approving something they did not. It is the clearest argument I have seen for limiting local administrator rights, and it does not require the audience to care about security to follow it.

Rob and I also take questions at the end on tracking local administrator account creation and on renaming the built-in Administrator account, which is a small change that removes an obvious first guess for anyone brute forcing a domain.

Presented · Syxsense Master Class

Spotlight: Realtime Management

No recording of this one. The writeup stands on its own.

A Syxsense Master Class, delivered as the vendor's technical presenter.

Realtime endpoint management and vulnerability management were the categories I spent the most time on at Syxsense, both in front of prospects and inside the product. The webinar was one part of that job. The rest was proofs of concept, architecture sessions, and RFI and RFP responses for customers in critical infrastructure and government, where the scanning and remediation story has to hold up against a regulator as well as a security team.

What it covers

The management console as a working surface rather than a feature tour, and what realtime actually means in practice. An agent that reports back on its own schedule, and a console that can act on what it reports without waiting for the next scan window.

Worth watching

The part where the console stops being a reporting tool. Seeing the state of an estate is the easy half. Being able to change that state from the same place, on the same day, is what separates this from a dashboard.
